extracted.intended_audience: researchers, librarians, and academics evaluating journals and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and checklists for recognizing, classifying, and responding to predatory journals and publishers; aimed at helping authors, reviewers, and institutions evaluate the legitimacy and quality of academic journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common characteristics of predatory publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints that are associated with predatory open-access publishing include: Accepting articles quickly with little or no peer review or quality control (including hoax and nonsensical papers); Notifying academics of article fees only after papers are accepted; Accepting papers which are outside of the declared scope of the journal; Aggressively campaigning for academics to submit articles or serve on editorial boards; Listing academics as members of editorial boards without their permission, and not allowing academics to resign from editorial boards; Appointing fake academics to editorial boards; Mimicking the name or web site style of more established journals; Making misleading claims about the publishing operation, such as providing false locations; Using ISSNs improperly; Citing fake or non-existent impact factors; Boasting about being "indexed" by academic social networking sites (like ResearchGate) and standard identifiers (like ISSNs and DOIs) as if they were prestigious or reputable bibliographic databases; Favoritism and self-promotion in peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consolidated list of red flags is presented in the article as common complaints and examples; presence of one sign does not prove predatory behaviour but multiple signs increase concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beall's criteria (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jeffrey Beall used a set of criteria to identify potentially predatory open-access publishers. In 2015 he used 26 criteria related to poor journal standards and practices, 9 related to journal editors and staff members, 7 related to ethics and integrity, 6 related to the publisher's business practices, and 6 'other' general criteria related to publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beall published his criteria and lists (Beall's List) and used them as an evaluative tool; his approach has been influential but also criticized for being subjective and for overgeneralizing; some items may apply to reputable but new or low-resource journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: publisher not member of recognized professional organisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher is not a member of any recognized professional organisation committed to best publishing practices (like COPE or EASE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Eriksson & Helgesson's 25 signs; they warn that meeting a single criterion does not make a journal predatory but the more signs present, the more sceptical one should be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: journal not indexed in established databases
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal is not indexed in well-established electronic databases (like MEDLINE or Web of Science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing in major, reputable databases is a positive indicator; lack of indexing is a potential warning sign, especially if other concerns are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: publisher claims to be 'leading' despite being new
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher claims to be a 'leading publisher' even though it just got started.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grandiose claims about reputation and leadership without supporting evidence are suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: unfamiliar journal/publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal and the publisher are unfamiliar to you and all your colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local subject-area awareness helps; unfamiliarity is a signal to investigate further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: poor research quality and pseudo-science
rubrics_metrics.description: The papers of the journal are of poor research quality, and may not be academic at all (for instance allowing for obvious pseudo-science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine sample articles for methodological quality, references, and academic standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: fundamental errors and repeated typos
rubrics_metrics.description: There are fundamental errors in the titles and abstracts, or frequent and repeated typographical or factual errors throughout the published papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent editorial sloppiness across issues is a warning sign of weak quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: unprofessional website
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal website is not professional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for broken links, poor layout, inconsistent information, and obvious template copying as indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: no editorial board or insufficient details
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal website does not present an editorial board or gives insufficient detail on names and affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify editorial board members independently; absence or vagueness is suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: editorial office location not revealed or incorrect
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal website does not reveal the journal's editorial office location or uses an incorrect address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False or vague contact details are a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: publishing schedule not clearly stated
rubrics_metrics.description: The publishing schedule is not clearly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity about frequency and timelines can indicate poor organization or deceptive practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: title claims national/international affiliation that mismatches location
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal title claims a national affiliation that does not match its location (such as 'American Journal of ...' while being located on another continent) or includes 'International' in its title while having a single-country editorial board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misleading geographic or scope claims merit scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: mimicking another journal title or website
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal mimics another journal title or the website of said journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare suspected sites with the legitimate journal; look for small differences in URLs, logos, or scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: providing an impact factor for a new journal
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal provides an impact factor in spite of the fact that the journal is new (which means that the impact cannot yet be calculated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check authoritative sources for impact factors; false claims are deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: claiming unrealistically high impact via spurious metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal claims an unrealistically high impact based on spurious alternative impact factors (such as 7 for a bioethics journal, which is far beyond the top notation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of invented or obscure metrics presented as authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: posting unrelated/non-academic advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal website posts non-related or non-academic advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive commercial content unrelated to scholarship suggests profit motive over quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: publisher releases overwhelmingly large suite of journals quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher of the journal has released an overwhelmingly large suite of new journals at one occasion or during a very short period of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid mass-creation of journals can indicate a publisher prioritizing revenue volume over quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: editor-in-chief holds same role across unrelated journals
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor in chief of the journal is editor in chief also for other journals with widely different focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unrealistic editorial commitments or fictitious editorial claims are suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: publishing articles far outside stated scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal includes articles (very far) outside its stated scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope-drift or indiscriminate acceptance suggests poor editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: unsolicited invitations outside expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal sends you an unsolicited invitation to submit an article for publication, while making it blatantly clear that the editor has absolutely no idea about your field of expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flattering but generic invitations are common spam tactics used by predatory journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: poor-quality emails from editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Emails from the journal editor are written in poor language, include exaggerated flattering, and make contradictory claims (such as 'You have to respond within 48 h' while later on saying 'You may submit your manuscript whenever you find convenient').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate solicitation emails for professionalism and internal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: charging submission/handling fees (not publication fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal charges a submission or handling fee, instead of a publication fee (which means that you have to pay even if the paper is not accepted for publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate open-access journals usually charge APCs on acceptance, not fees merely to submit; unclear fee schemes are a warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: fees and amounts not clearly stated
rubrics_metrics.description: The types of submission/publication fees and what they amount to are not clearly stated on the journal's website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent fee policies are expected of reputable publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: unrealistic promises about peer-review speed or track-record
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal gives unrealistic promises regarding the speed of the peer review process (hinting that the journal's peer review process is minimal or non-existent)—or boasts an equally unrealistic track-record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very rapid acceptance timelines often indicate inadequate peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: unclear or demanding copyright policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal does not describe copyright agreements clearly or demands the copyright of the paper while claiming to be an open-access journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusing or exploitative copyright terms are a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eriksson & Helgesson: no misconduct/conflict/archiving strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal displays no strategies for how to handle misconduct, conflicts of interest, or secure the archiving of articles when no longer in operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputable journals have policies for misconduct, COI, retractions, and digital preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: scope too broad or inconsistent
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope is too broad or inconsistent, e.g., it covers both biomedical and non-biomedical topics, irrespective of the title of the journal. They publish special issues on topics that are clearly outside the scope of the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether published content matches stated aims and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: accept all submitted papers and fake peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: They accept all submitted papers and pretend to have a peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check acceptance rates and whether peer review reports or editorial decisions are documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: no reputable affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: They are not affiliated with any reputable organization or university.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of legitimate institutional ties can be a warning sign, though some independent journals are legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: published papers are poor quality and many per issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The published papers are of poor quality because they have never been peer-reviewed or edited. In most of the cases, they publish a large number of papers per issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High volume per issue combined with low editorial standards suggests prioritizing revenue over quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: inviting researchers outside the journal's scope
rubrics_metrics.description: They invite researchers to submit manuscripts with expertise in fields that are clearly outside the scope of the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic mass-mailing to irrelevant scholars indicates spam solicitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: false/misleading indexing claims
rubrics_metrics.description: They state false or misleading information about their indexing service(s) and/or are indexed in irrelevant agencies or not indexed in relevant databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify indexing claims with the named services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: falsify impact factors or similar metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: They falsify the information about their impact factors or similar metrics. Most of these journals claim to have an impact factor, despite being too new to have one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check impact factor claims against Clarivate/Web of Science or other authoritative sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: false/misleading editorial board information
rubrics_metrics.description: They state false or misleading information about its editorial board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify editorial members' affiliations and whether they consent to serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: hidden or misleading fees
rubrics_metrics.description: They state false or misleading information about the costs involved in publishing with them or authors are surprised to discover hidden fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent fee schedules should be posted; hidden fees are a common predatory tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: not monitored by or member of recognised organisations
rubrics_metrics.description: They are not monitored by or member of a regional or international organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership in industry bodies (COPE, DOAJ, OASPA, etc.) is a positive signal but not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: no misconduct/retraction policy
rubrics_metrics.description: They have no information about the strategy for handling misconduct (such as plagiarism, salami slicing, or a retraction policy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for clear policies on plagiarism detection, corrections and retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: website not up-to-date or lacking submission/processing info
rubrics_metrics.description: The website is either not up-to-date or lacks important information about submission requirements and manuscript processing and reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-maintained and informative websites are typical of reputable journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: manuscript submission via email or basic site
rubrics_metrics.description: The manuscripts are submitted through the email of the journal or directly on the journal's website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While submission systems vary, professional submission platforms and documented workflows are common for established journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memon criterion: lack of contact details or false location information
rubrics_metrics.description: They do not usually mention the contact details. There is also false or misleading information about the location of the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify contact addresses and institutional affiliations; false locations are a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scopus criterion: substantially higher self-citation rate (outlier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scopus automatically flags a journal that is an outlier in two consecutive years according to any of three criteria comparing it with peer journals in its subject field: Substantially higher self-citation rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive self-citation can be a metric used to identify journals gaming citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scopus criterion: substantially lower citation counts (outlier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scopus flag: Substantially lower number of citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very low citation performance relative to peer journals may indicate low impact or visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scopus criterion: substantially lower CiteScore (outlier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scopus flag: Substantially lower CiteScore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low bibliometric scores relative to peers may prompt further review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web of Science check: excessive citations of works authored by board members
rubrics_metrics.description: Web of Science checks for excessive citations of the works authored by the journal board members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unusual citation patterns involving board members can indicate citation manipulation or nepotistic citation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus 2019 definition of predatory journals/publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory journals and publishers are entities that prioritize self-interest at the expense of scholarship and are characterized by false or misleading information, deviation from best editorial and publication practices, a lack of transparency, and/or the use of aggressive and indiscriminate solicitation practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consensus definition (Ottawa 2019) is intended to unify understanding; note that it intentionally did not include 'adequacy of peer review' because of subjectivity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: InterAcademy Partnership classification (types of problematic journals)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed classification distinguishing: (a) hijacked journals (mimicking reputable journals); (b) journals which re-publish papers from legitimate journals; (c) journals which deceive potential authors by giving false or misleading information about charges/services/identity; (d) low-quality journals characterised by poor cumulative criteria without apparent deceitful intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes a spectrum — some outlets are outright frauds while others are low-quality or opportunistic. A journal may belong to multiple categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Transparency and Best Practice (COPE/DOAJ/OASPA/WAME)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles of transparency and best practice in scholarly publishing (issued collectively by COPE, DOAJ, OASPA, and WAME) set out criteria to 'set apart legitimate journals and publishers from non-legitimate ones'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult these jointly issued principles as a positive checklist for reputable publishing practice (e.g., transparent fees, declared editorial policies, COI and retraction policies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blacklists and whitelists — cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Blacklists (e.g., Beall's List, Cabell's Predatory Reports) and whitelists (e.g., DOAJ) have been used to identify unacceptable or acceptable journals, but COPE recommends against blindly trusting any list, especially if they do not publish evaluation criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists can be helpful but may be subjective, incomplete, or unfairly exclude legitimate new or resource-limited journals; always check underlying criteria and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical stings as evidentiary demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations (e.g., Bohannon's flawed-paper experiment; Anna O. Szust "Dr Fraud" experiment; SCIgen paper acceptances) demonstrate that many journals accepted obviously flawed or fake submissions, revealing failures in claimed peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical stings highlight patterns (rapid acceptance, lack of real peer review) and should inform skepticism, but they are not a formal checklist item for every journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predatory score / objective discriminating metrics (proposals)
rubrics_metrics.description: More objective discriminating metrics have been proposed, such as a 'predatory score' and positive and negative journal quality indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative scoring systems aim to reduce subjectivity; these remain proposals and should be used in combination with qualitative judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice: improve publication literacy and institutional policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures suggested to combat predatory journals include improving publication literacy (especially among junior researchers in developing countries), funder policies on acceptable journals, and institution-level guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education and clear institutional/funder policies (e.g., accepted indexes) reduce vulnerability to predatory practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign: Think. Check. Submit.
rubrics_metrics.description: An awareness campaign encouraging authors to verify journals before submitting (Think. Check. Submit.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use campaign checklists as a practical pre-submission rubric (verify editorial board, indexing, peer-review process, fees, contact details).
